<div class="wrap">

  <header>
    <div class="eyebrow">occJSDM &middot; validation &middot; 29 July 2026</div>
    <h1>Checking whether the model&rsquo;s uncertainty is honest</h1>
    <p class="standfirst">
      A plain-language guide to the test suite: what it does, what
      &ldquo;coverage&rdquo; means, and what happened when the study was re-run
      after the first round of fixes.
    </p>
  </header>

  <section>
    <h2>The trick behind every test</h2>
    <p>
      All of it rests on one idea: <strong>make fake data where we already know the
      right answer.</strong> <code>simulateOccJSDMData()</code> lets us choose the true
      species coefficients, the true detection rates, the true everything &mdash; then
      generate a dataset from them.
    </p>
    <p>
      We hand that dataset to <code>runOccJSDM()</code>, which knows none of it, and
      check whether it finds its way back. Real data can never do this. You never know
      the true occupancy of a species at a site, so you can never tell whether the model
      got it right.
    </p>
  </section>

  <section>
    <h2>What &ldquo;coverage&rdquo; means</h2>
    <p>
      The model doesn&rsquo;t just report a number for, say, species 3&rsquo;s response
      to elevation. It reports a <strong>95% credible interval</strong> &mdash; a range,
      with the claim <em>&ldquo;I&rsquo;m 95% sure the true value is in here.&rdquo;</em>
    </p>
    <p>
      That claim is testable. Simulate 100 datasets where the truth is known, fit all
      100, and for each ask one question: did the interval contain the truth? Then count.
      That count is <strong>coverage</strong>. Falling short of the advertised rate is
      <strong>undercoverage</strong> &mdash; intervals that contain the truth less often
      than they promise, because they are too narrow or sitting off-centre.
    </p>
    <p>
      It matters in print. Report a 95% interval for a parameter that covers at 72%, and
      you are overstating your confidence to a reader who has no way to check.
      Overcoverage &mdash; intervals wider than they need to be &mdash; is the opposite
      problem: safer, but you are discarding power you actually had.
    </p>
  </section>

  <section>
    <h2>The study has now been run twice</h2>
    <p>
      The first run, in late July, found several parameters whose intervals were not
      honest. Those results were traced to specific lines of code, some of which have
      since been fixed. The study was then re-run to find out whether the fixes worked.
    </p>
    <p>
      <strong>The two runs used identical simulated data.</strong> Each dataset is
      generated from a seed derived from its scenario and replicate number, so the
      second run recreated the first run&rsquo;s 1000 datasets exactly &mdash; verified,
      not assumed. Every difference below is therefore caused by the change in code, not
      by the luck of a different draw. Each square is one dataset; the faded row is
      before, the solid row after.
    </p>

    <div class="tally-set">

      <figure class="tally">
        <div class="tally-head">
          <div class="tally-label">
            <b>Collection covariates</b> &mdash; moved, but nowhere near far enough
          </div>
          <div class="tally-delta">72 &rarr; 76 of 100</div>
        </div>
        <div class="tally-row">
          <div class="tally-when">before</div>
          <div class="marks is-before" data-hits="72"></div>
          <div class="tally-score is-bad">0.717</div>
        </div>
        <div class="tally-row">
          <div class="tally-when">after</div>
          <div class="marks" data-hits="76"></div>
          <div class="tally-score is-bad">0.763</div>
        </div>
        <figcaption class="tally-note">
          The fix was real &mdash; two-thirds of the bias is gone &mdash; but a
          &ldquo;95%&rdquo; interval that behaves like a 76% one is still not honest.
          Something else is wrong.
        </figcaption>
      </figure>

      <figure class="tally">
        <div class="tally-head">
          <div class="tally-label">
            <b>Species correlations</b> &mdash; did not move at all
          </div>
          <div class="tally-delta">76 &rarr; 76 of 100</div>
        </div>
        <div class="tally-row">
          <div class="tally-when">before</div>
          <div class="marks is-before" data-hits="76"></div>
          <div class="tally-score is-bad">0.763</div>
        </div>
        <div class="tally-row">
          <div class="tally-when">after</div>
          <div class="marks" data-hits="76"></div>
          <div class="tally-score is-bad">0.763</div>
        </div>
        <figcaption class="tally-note">
          Across the whole study, only 104 of 49,978 individual checks changed their
          answer. The cause of this one has not been fixed, and the identical result on
          identical data says so unambiguously.
        </figcaption>
      </figure>

      <figure class="tally">
        <div class="tally-head">
          <div class="tally-label">
            <b>Environmental effects</b> &mdash; what an honest interval looks like
          </div>
          <div class="tally-delta">94 &rarr; 95 of 100</div>
        </div>
        <div class="tally-row">
          <div class="tally-when">before</div>
          <div class="marks is-before" data-hits="94"></div>
          <div class="tally-score is-good">0.943</div>
        </div>
        <div class="tally-row">
          <div class="tally-when">after</div>
          <div class="marks" data-hits="95"></div>
          <div class="tally-score is-good">0.947</div>
        </div>
        <figcaption class="tally-note">
          Close to the promised 95 both times. The interval means what it says, and the
          fixes did not disturb it.
        </figcaption>
      </figure>

    </div>
  </section>

  <section>
    <h2>Why exactly 100 datasets</h2>
    <p>
      Coverage is a proportion, so it carries sampling error like any other estimate.
      With 100 datasets the standard error is about <strong>2.2 percentage
      points</strong>. So a gap of 0.94 against 0.95 is noise and means nothing; a gap
      of 0.72 against 0.95 is ten standard errors and means a great deal.
    </p>
    <p>
      With only five datasets the error is nearer eight points, and 0.78 cannot be
      distinguished from 0.95 at all. That is precisely why the quick daily check
      can&rsquo;t answer this question and the long run can.
    </p>
  </section>

  <section>
    <h2>Three tiers, by what they cost</h2>
    <div class="tiers">
      <div class="tier">
        <div class="tier-when">7&nbsp;sec<br>every&nbsp;run</div>
        <div class="tier-body">
          <h3>Does it work at all?</h3>
          <p>
            Fits every configuration the package offers &mdash; two-stage, occupancy-only,
            pure JSDM, with and without traits or spatial structure &mdash; and checks each
            completes and returns sensibly shaped output. Also one test per bug already
            fixed, named after it, so none comes back unnoticed.
          </p>
          <p>
            Checks <em>shape</em> rather than exact numbers. That rule was originally
            forced: a threading bug meant the same seed gave different answers on
            different machines. That is now fixed &mdash; the model reproduces exactly
            from a seed &mdash; but the rule stays, for a better reason. Any legitimate
            change to the sampler moves every number, and a suite full of stored values
            would turn each such change into a wall of failures that says nothing about
            whether anything is actually broken.
          </p>
        </div>
      </div>

      <div class="tier">
        <div class="tier-when">30&nbsp;sec<br>local&nbsp;only</div>
        <div class="tier-body">
          <h3>Has anything obviously broken?</h3>
          <p>
            Five simulated datasets, fitted and compared against their known truth. Too
            few to measure coverage &mdash; it&rsquo;s a canary. Its real job is catching a
            broken connection between &ldquo;true value&rdquo; and &ldquo;estimated
            value&rdquo;, which would show up as coverage near zero rather than merely low.
          </p>
        </div>
      </div>

      <div class="tier">
        <div class="tier-when">4.75&nbsp;hr<br>on&nbsp;demand</div>
        <div class="tier-body">
          <h3>Is the model&rsquo;s uncertainty honest?</h3>
          <p>
            One hundred simulated datasets for each of ten scenarios. This is the coverage
            study, and the only tier that can answer the question above. The most recent
            run took 285 minutes across five processor cores and fitted the model 1000
            times without a single failure.
          </p>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  </section>

  <section>
    <h2>The ten scenarios</h2>
    <p>
      One is the reference design; the other nine each change <strong>exactly one
      thing</strong> about it. When a cell misbehaves, you know which feature caused it.
    </p>
    <p>
      The reference is a mid-sized survey: 100 sites, 10 species, 2 water samples per
      site, 2 primers, 3 PCR replicates each, two environmental covariates, one
      collection covariate, two measured traits, two ordination axes, spatial field on.
      It exercises every feature at once.
    </p>

    <div class="scroller">
      <table>
        <caption>Each variant differs from the reference in one respect only.</caption>
        <thead>
          <tr><th>Scenario</th><th>What changes</th><th>What it asks</th></tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr><td class="name">spatial_isolated</td><td>traits off</td><td>Does the spatial term work with trait effects out of the way?</td></tr>
          <tr><td class="name">traits_isolated</td><td>spatial off</td><td>Does the trait&times;environment term work without the spatial field competing?</td></tr>
          <tr><td class="name">primers_3</td><td>2 &rarr; 3 primers</td><td>Does per-primer detection hold with more primers?</td></tr>
          <tr><td class="name">low_information</td><td>40 sites, weak detection</td><td>The hard case: thin, realistic eDNA data.</td></tr>
          <tr><td class="name">d_underfit</td><td>truth 4 axes, fit 2</td><td>Under-specifying the ordination &mdash; the common real mistake.</td></tr>
          <tr><td class="name">d_overfit</td><td>truth 2 axes, fit 4</td><td>Over-specifying it.</td></tr>
          <tr><td class="name">species_20</td><td>10 &rarr; 20 species</td><td>Does it hold as the community grows?</td></tr>
          <tr><td class="name">occupancy</td><td>no PCR stage</td><td>The collapsed form: field replicates only.</td></tr>
          <tr><td class="name">binary</td><td>no replicates</td><td>Pure JSDM, no detection model.</td></tr>
        </tbody>
      </table>
    </div>

    <p>
      Testing every <em>combination</em> would be roughly fifty cells and days of
      compute. The cost of changing one thing at a time is that it can&rsquo;t see two
      features that each work alone but break together. The reference design is the
      exception: it runs traits and spatial simultaneously, so it covers the interaction
      most likely to matter, since both write into the same equation.
    </p>
  </section>

  <section>
    <h2>Where things stand after the fixes</h2>
    <p>
      Ten scenarios, 100 simulated datasets each, no failures &mdash; 155,578
      individual interval checks. Read against the 2.2-point standard error:
      anything from 0.93 to 0.97 is indistinguishable from correct.
    </p>

    <div class="scroller">
      <table>
        <caption>Coverage by parameter and scenario, after the fixes. Red = intervals too narrow. Blue = wider than needed. Dash = not estimated in that design.</caption>
        <thead>
          <tr>
            <th>What it is</th><th>base</th><th>spatial<br>only</th><th>traits<br>only</th>
            <th>3 primers</th><th>weak<br>data</th><th>too few<br>axes</th><th>too many<br>axes</th>
            <th>20 spp</th><th>occup.</th><th>JSDM</th>
          </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr><td>Species intercepts</td><td class="num">0.948</td><td class="num">0.943</td><td class="num">0.942</td><td class="num">0.954</td><td class="num lo">0.862</td><td class="num">0.958</td><td class="num">0.950</td><td class="num">0.951</td><td class="num">0.953</td><td class="num">0.962</td></tr>
          <tr><td>Environmental effects</td><td class="num">0.947</td><td class="num lo">0.883</td><td class="num">0.916</td><td class="num">0.942</td><td class="num lo">0.826</td><td class="num">0.936</td><td class="num">0.939</td><td class="num">0.933</td><td class="num">0.947</td><td class="num">0.952</td></tr>
          <tr><td>Trait &times; environment</td><td class="num">0.948</td><td class="num">&mdash;</td><td class="num">0.945</td><td class="num hi">0.975</td><td class="num lo">0.840</td><td class="num">0.953</td><td class="num">0.955</td><td class="num">0.925</td><td class="num hi">0.970</td><td class="num">0.938</td></tr>
          <tr><td>Stage&nbsp;2 false positives</td><td class="num">0.945</td><td class="num">0.947</td><td class="num">0.949</td><td class="num">0.937</td><td class="num">0.911</td><td class="num">0.946</td><td class="num">0.943</td><td class="num">0.950</td><td class="num">&mdash;</td><td class="num">&mdash;</td></tr>
          <tr class="flag"><td>Stage&nbsp;1 contamination</td><td class="num hi">0.983</td><td class="num hi">0.983</td><td class="num hi">0.978</td><td class="num hi">0.985</td><td class="num lo">0.602</td><td class="num hi">0.980</td><td class="num hi">0.981</td><td class="num hi">0.982</td><td class="num hi">0.985</td><td class="num">&mdash;</td></tr>
          <tr class="flag"><td>Stage&nbsp;2 detection</td><td class="num">0.902</td><td class="num">0.911</td><td class="num">0.900</td><td class="num">0.925</td><td class="num lo">0.109</td><td class="num">0.913</td><td class="num">0.919</td><td class="num">0.908</td><td class="num">&mdash;</td><td class="num">&mdash;</td></tr>
          <tr class="flag"><td>Species correlations</td><td class="num lo">0.763</td><td class="num lo">0.758</td><td class="num lo">0.758</td><td class="num lo">0.768</td><td class="num lo">0.764</td><td class="num hi">0.980</td><td class="num lo">0.755</td><td class="num lo">0.752</td><td class="num lo">0.761</td><td class="num lo">0.752</td></tr>
          <tr class="flag"><td>Stage&nbsp;1 collection covariates</td><td class="num lo">0.763</td><td class="num lo">0.762</td><td class="num lo">0.771</td><td class="num lo">0.718</td><td class="num hi">0.983</td><td class="num lo">0.750</td><td class="num lo">0.752</td><td class="num lo">0.727</td><td class="num lo">0.709</td><td class="num">&mdash;</td></tr>
        </tbody>

    <h3>What holds</h3>
    <p>
      Species intercepts, environmental effects, the trait&times;environment
      (fourth-corner) term and the Stage&nbsp;2 false-positive rate all land at
      or near nominal in every scenario but one. The quantities most likely to
      be reported in an ecology paper can be quoted as they stand &mdash; with one
      caveat, below, about how far the species intercepts sit from the truth.
    </p>

    <h3>What was fixed, and what wasn&rsquo;t</h3>
    <p>
      <strong>Collection covariates: better, not fixed.</strong> The prior for these
      coefficients was centred on 1 rather than 0, pulling every estimate upward. That
      has been corrected, and it helped &mdash; every scenario gained three to five
      points and two-thirds of the bias disappeared. But coverage is still 0.71 to 0.77,
      and the remainder has the same signature as before: flat across model type, primer
      count, species count and ordination misspecification. A fault that doesn&rsquo;t
      vary with the data is in the code, not the data. There is a second cause still to
      find.
    </p>
    <p>
      <strong>Species correlations: unchanged, because the cause is unchanged.</strong>
      A rescaling step preserves the model&rsquo;s predictions but silently changes the
      correlation matrix computed from them, inflating correlations toward
      &plusmn;1. It has not been altered, and the re-run confirms the consequence
      precisely: identical data in, identical coverage out. The exception remains
      informative &mdash; where the model is given too few ordination axes, coverage
      rises to 0.98, because the intervals widen enough to hide the problem. A fit with
      too few factors looks better calibrated than it is.
    </p>

    <h3>The one that turned out not to be a bug</h3>
    <p>
      Stage&nbsp;2 detection still collapses to 0.11 in the weak-data scenario, against
      0.90 elsewhere. The first version of this page called that a fault in the prior.
      <strong>That was wrong, and worth correcting plainly.</strong>
    </p>
    <p>
      In this model the true detection rate and the false-positive rate enter the
      likelihood symmetrically: nothing in the equations distinguishes &ldquo;present and
      usually detected&rdquo; from &ldquo;absent and often contaminated&rdquo;. The
      informative prior is what breaks that tie. Flatten it and the model is not
      better calibrated &mdash; it is unidentified, free to settle on either explanation.
      The earlier experiment that appeared to fix coverage only worked because the two
      rates happened to be far apart in that scenario.
    </p>
    <p>
      So this cell is not measuring a defect. It is measuring the price of an assumption
      the model needs in order to mean anything at all, in the regime where that
      assumption is least comfortable. The open question is not <em>how do we remove
      it</em> but <em>how strong should it be</em> &mdash; a modelling judgement, and one
      users should be told about when their detection rates are genuinely low.
    </p>
  </section>

  <section>
    <h2>Two things the re-run turned up</h2>

    <div class="finding">
      <h3>Species intercepts drifted, and coverage never showed it</h3>
      <p>
        On identical data, the average distance between the estimated species intercepts
        and their true values roughly doubled between the two runs, in nine of the ten
        scenarios. Coverage stayed put at 0.94, because the intervals are wide enough to
        absorb the shift &mdash; so nothing in the table above reveals it.
      </p>
      <p>
        This is a good argument for tracking how far estimates sit from the truth
        alongside whether the intervals cover it. The two answer different questions, and
        here only one of them noticed. None of the fixes should have moved species
        intercepts; the likely culprit is a large rewrite that arrived in the same batch,
        and it needs a cause before these numbers appear in a paper.
      </p>
    </div>

    <div class="finding">
      <h3>Stage&nbsp;1 contamination now overshoots</h3>
      <p>
        This parameter used to sit close to nominal, between 0.94 and 0.96. It now covers
        at 0.98 in nine scenarios &mdash; intervals wider than they need to be. The
        likely cause is the same edit that corrected the collection-covariate prior,
        which also widened its variance, and appears to have widened it too far.
      </p>
      <p>
        Overcoverage is the safe direction, so this is not urgent. But it is a reminder
        that a fix can overshoot as easily as it can fall short, and that both directions
        are worth watching.
      </p>
    </div>
  </section>

  <section>
    <h2>Where this leaves the package</h2>
    <div class="pending">
      <p>
        Of the three problems the first study found, one is partly fixed, one is
        untouched, and one turned out not to be a problem at all. The re-run added two
        more. Every one is recorded with the measurement that identified it, so nothing
        rests on recollection.
      </p>
      <p>
        None of this was visible from reading the code. An audit had already been over
        these files and walked past all of it. It took a study that could say
        <em>which</em> parameters were miscalibrated before the causes became findable
        &mdash; and a second run on the same data before the fixes could be told apart
        from noise.
      </p>
    </div>
  </section>

  <footer>
    Two parameters are deliberately absent from every table: the spatial length-scale and
    the factor-score variance. Neither is currently recoverable, both are recorded as open
    bugs, and reporting a coverage figure for either would be misleading rather than merely
    uninformative. One further parameter, the residual variance, reads as perfect coverage
    everywhere because its prior dominates by construction &mdash; not because it is well
    estimated.
  </footer>

</div>
</div>

<script>
(function () {
  // Lay out each tally as 100 marks. Misses are spread by a fixed stride
  // rather than randomised, so the figures stay visually comparable and the
  // page renders identically every time. Scoped to this article's marks only.
  document.querySelectorAll('.occjsdm-report .marks').forEach(function (el) {
    var hits = parseInt(el.dataset.hits, 10);
    var misses = 100 - hits;
    var stride = misses > 0 ? 100 / misses : Infinity;
    var next = stride / 2;
    var frag = document.createDocumentFragment();

    for (var i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
      var d = document.createElement('div');
      var isMiss = misses > 0 && i >= Math.floor(next);
      if (isMiss) { next += stride; }
      d.className = 'mark ' + (isMiss ? 'miss' : 'hit');
      frag.appendChild(d);
    }
    el.appendChild(frag);
  });
})();
</script>
